articles.title: ARTEX, and the offensive tool powered by LLMjacking five months earlier
articles.context: The Sysdig TRT has a name for the kind of operator these tools enable: An agentic threat actor (ATA) is an operator whose attack capability is delivered via an AI agent rather...
articles.full_text:
On June 12, 2026, the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) watched someone build an autonomous hacking tool using someone else’s AI server. Then, in July, a similar tool called ARTEX appeared on GitHub. On November 13, the FBI released a FLASH saying a variety of threat actors have been running ARTEX against several business sectors.

To be clear, there is no proof to date linking these two offensive tools. However, they are similar in nature, have both been documented as using LLMjacking to power AI inference, and defenders can learn from both about why they shouldn’t underestimate their speed, cost, or ability.

The Sysdig TRT has a name for the kind of operator these tools enable: An agentic threat actor (ATA) is an operator whose attack capability is delivered via an AI agent rather than a human at the keyboard. ARTEX is the newest entry.

This blog covers what each tool did and what defenders can learn from putting them side by side.

What the Sysdig Threat Research Team documented in June

Over the summer, the Sysdig TRT saw someone using a misconfigured Ollama server as the reasoning engine to build an automated, multi-stage offensive tool. The actor wasn't chatting with the model or reselling access as seen in prior LLMjacking operations. Instead, they wired it into a pipeline that scanned a target, matched it to known vulnerabilities, wrote proofs-of-concept (PoCs), and tried to break in, with the model making the decisions at every step. The tool self-identified throughout the code as VAPT, shorthand for vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, so we dubbed the tool VAPT.

Because VAPT sent its full instructions to the model on every request, we captured the whole architecture: fingerprinting, vulnerability matching, web recon, PoC synthesis, SQL injection, credential extraction, privilege escalation, and an orchestrator that ran until it got command execution. VAPT was being rewritten stage by stage while the Sysdig TRT watched, and every target was a private practice range. We were looking at a tool in development, before it was potentially turned on real victims.

Due to LLMjacking, the Ollama server was free, unauthenticated, and unmetered. For an actor whose tool makes hundreds of model calls per attack, our blog said, "the economics are clear." When the cost of an attack drops to the cost of inference, and inference is stolen, offensive operations become free.

What is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open source, multi-agent penetration testing platform written in Go. It turns the operator’s goals written in natural language into machine commands run by specialized AI agents, with minimal human involvement necessary beyond setting the objective.

ARTEX doesn’t have a model of its own. Microsoft describes its architecture as a planner agent to decide next steps and worker agents to run command tools, with all of the findings compiled in a shared graph of assets and vulnerabilities. A prominent ARTEX campaign analyzed by Amazon Threat Intelligence was powered by the large-scale theft of credentials used to access AI models. Attackers organized a self-sustaining LLMjacking operation in which stolen keys paid for the AI inference to drive further credential hunting.

Fortunately, the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) in the FBI FLASH read like an attack playbook every security team already knows:

Sub-second permission checks and dry-runs

Exploitation of SAML, XXE, SSRF, injection flaws, and hardcoded credentials

Web shells and open source remote access trojans (RATs) for persistence

Kerberoasting and DCSync for escalation

Residential proxies, Tor, and tunneling tools used for command and control (C2)

The FBI says ARTEX traffic is noisy, which means defense evasion techniques aren’t an issue. It’s the speed that can pose a problem. Some intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours, though according to Microsoft, most targeting attempts were unsuccessful. While other campaigns move faster with more success, three hours is nothing to brush off.

What VAPT has in common with ARTEX

The "authorized pentest" label is a master key. That framing recurred across VAPT's stages, and the operator likely used it as a wrapper to keep the model cooperative, even though the AI model was already abliterated, or had the guardrails removed. Whether VAPT was truly created for educational purposes or not, the compute engine used to build it was stolen. Therefore, the entire campaign was unauthorized.

The FBI FLASH says attackers favor models with a "lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing." Call the job a pentest, and many AI models stop asking questions. That's not one provider's bug, but a dual-use problem without a clean technical fix.

To that end, VAPT's first probes asked for an abliterated Llama-3.3-70B model. Its model list also included deepseek-r1:8b. The FBI says ARTEX operators gravitate to the DeepSeek Flash family because of its "balance of capabilities, relatively low cost, and lack of observable guardrails." Different models, but the selection criteria are the same: capable enough (they don’t need to be frontier models), cheap, and not likely to refuse a prompt.

VAPT's operator simply repointed a backend-agnostic tool at a free Ollama server in place of paid OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google APIs. ARTEX has no model of its own and plugs into at least six providers. In both cases, changing the engine is a configuration change. That's why "just block the bad model" isn't a strategy — it would require blocking all the models, and that just isn’t logical.

Another similarity is that neither VAPT nor ARTEX needs a novel exploit. There was no CVE in the VAPT operation, and the FLASH cites none for ARTEX either. The speed comes from chaining ordinary weaknesses without getting tired or pausing efforts. These AI-powered tools industrialize the boring stuff. And when pitted against human defenders, those who have to eat and sleep will always be at a disadvantage.

Lastly, both the tools and their fuel are sitting in the open. Researchers previously catalogued roughly 175,000 publicly exposed Ollama instances. And as of early November, researchers counted over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles, according to the FBI. One is a free engine. The other is the thing the engine drives. The attackers have the same hygiene problem as the people they target.

Where VAPT and ARTEX differ

VAPT (June)

ARTEX (July onward)

Who

One actor on residential IP space in India

A variety of actors

What it is

One actor's tool, iterated within a session

An open source project with thousands of forks, translations, and a commercial edition

Targets

Private practice ranges

Real organizations across many sectors

Where the compute came from

Documented. An exposed and unmonitored server

Not established

What defenders saw

The tool's full instructions, because the model server was one we could observe

The aftermath: bursts, dry-runs, new credentials, webhooks

The last row is particularly important. With VAPT, the Sysdig TRT saw the brain. With ARTEX, defenders mostly see what the brain did. Behavior-based detection exists for exactly this reason.

Cost is an important part of the story

Defenders can change many things, but the price of an attacker's tokens isn't one of them.

Sysdig TRT’s LLMjacking research has followed this cost curve since 2024. That May, we coined the term for attackers using stolen cloud credentials to reach a victim's paid AI models, leaving the victim with the bill, and modeled a worst case of up to $46,000 per day. By 2025, LLMjacking had matured into an industrialized black market. In June came the next step: exposed model capacity powering an offensive tool. The economics of compute theft can now fund the development of offensive capabilities.

One month later, ARTEX showed up, and the FBI's advisory reads like a footnote for LLMjacking:

Model choice followed price. DeepSeek Flash dominates attacker-controlled instances partly because of its "relatively low cost."

Resellers and gateways are in the picture. The FLASH's one domain indicator is an LLM API reseller used in the South Korean campaign, and it tells defenders to hunt for LLM gateway software (CLIProxyAPI, New API).

The FBI wants your AI bill. Among the evidence it asks victims for: token consumption patterns or API billing anomalies, unfamiliar LLM proxies or resellers in egress logs, and outbound connections to LLM APIs.

It’s important to note that it doesn’t say "stolen" credentials or access, because a reseller isn't proof of theft. However, LLMjacking is a natural fuel for tools like ARTEX, and the credential-theft half of one intrusion can supply the compute for the next.

During a recent incident in October, the attacker used a harness similar to ARTEX and ran up a bill of $740,000 in unauthorized spend on stolen AI keys.

Separately, but further proving the point about what offensive security costs, Calif says it spent under $200 in tokens to find and build the first exploit for Java4Shell.

The AI bill is telemetry that very few organizations pay attention to, or monitor in real time. An owner of an exposed model server sees elevated compute and an open port, not realizing it’s a multi-stage attack pipeline. A victim of stolen AI credentials sees an invoice. The FBI asking for token consumption in incident reports should be a pretty obvious hint about where defenders should be looking.

The challenge of “dual use” tools

Herein lies the struggle with many open source tools and attacks. ARTEX's developer said the tool was for authorized security testing within defined scopes. And the intent behind VAPT was unclear, because it could’ve been developed and used for legitimate activity, but stealing compute was illegal either way.

The attack and the pentest are the same software, pointed at different targets. The "authorized" label works on the model, the repository gets pulled after abuse reports, and the forks keep going. The FBI says ARTEX still circulates through forks, archives, translations, and a commercial version. A GitHub query on November 18 returned around 1,100 repos, a few of which had thousands of forks. But blaming open source software isn’t the answer. And the transparency of open source software helps defenders to better understand the signals created by the tools themselves.

The defender’s playbook against autonomous hacking tools

Defenders worried about VAPT, ARTEX, and whatever nefarious autonomous offensive tool may come next can follow these recommendations. For ARTEX specifically, the FBI FLASH includes IOCs to hunt for as well.

Treat AI infrastructure like a database. Don't leave model servers on public interfaces without authentication, and watch their usage. An exposed Ollama server is someone else's free engine.

Add the AI bill to your telemetry. Alert on token consumption spikes, unfamiliar API consumers, and billing anomalies, and know which credentials grant model access.

Treat AI-service credentials like cloud credentials. They're a high-priority target and a currency. Rotate and scope them, and keep them out of repos.

Run authorized agentic testing against yourself first, and treat any open-source pentest harness you run as hostile code: isolate it from production and enforce scope in configuration, not prompts.

Detect behavior, not models. You can't predict which model sits behind the next tool. What you can see is the pace: sub-second permission checks, bursts with small changes, sequential enumeration on partner portals, new identities probing other tenants, and servers reaching webhook.site or LLM APIs they never used before.

Vet indicators before you block. Cloud-hosted IPs can be reassigned, so make sure you verify the list and periodically review your block list. They don’t need to be permanently banned.

Conclusion

In June, the Sysdig TRT watched someone build an offensive tool on borrowed compute and aim it at practice targets. In November, the FBI described a polished, open source offensive tool in the field, run by a variety of actors against real organizations. There is no clear link between the two aside from the fact that both have been documented using LLMjacking and neither required much money, skill, or novelty.

For two years, the question was whether AI agents could hack. That’s settled: they most definitely can. The question now is whether an organization will notice if they’re the one paying for it.

Check out the latest in threat research from the Sysdig TRT

articles.title: Who's accountable when the worker is an agent?
articles.context: I'll be working through these questions with Richard Smith, Founder of Codification and Alessandro Lo Prete from Sysdig's Threat Research Team on the panel at Ground Truth:...
articles.full_text:
This post is written by guest author Matt Adams, VP and Head of AI Security for Sapiens, who will be participating with us in the Ground Truth London event on AI workload security.

If you work for an organisation and something goes wrong on your watch, you know you're accountable. You have an employment contract, and if you get something badly wrong, there are consequences. Most of us rarely think about that, but a lot of security depends on it. An acceptable use policy, for example, works largely because people know someone will ask questions if they ignore it.

An agent doesn't care about any of that. It has a goal, and it will do whatever it can, to the best of its ability, to reach it. Usually there's no malice involved. It simply has no stake in what happens once the task is done.

The question I keep putting to security leaders is what takes the place of accountability when an agent is doing the work?

Finding what's actually running

Accountability starts with knowing who, or what, is doing the work. A couple of years ago, in one heavily regulated organisation I worked in, that was largely taken care of for us. The web filters were strict enough that AI services weren't reachable unless they'd been explicitly allowed through. Nobody could get to them, so there was nothing to inventory.

Few organisations are in that position now, so the first job is to go and look for the processes that are running and the data that's leaving.

Some of what you're looking for won't look like software at all. In many of the organisations I've spoken to, someone has written a skill or a prompt that works well for a task and shared it with colleagues. Sometimes that goes through a review before it's published, sometimes it's a Markdown file sent over chat. A lot of what drives these tools is plain text, and that makes a problem much harder to spot than an unfamiliar executable would be. After all, a risky instruction file and someone's meeting notes can look much the same.

Boil it down, and you can't hold anything to account before you know it exists. A useful inventory also records who is behind each agent, because that person is where the accountability still sits. In my experience, security leaders most often underestimate how widely AI is already being used, which is why inventory must come first.

Watching from outside the agent

Once you know what's running, the harder question is how you keep it within bounds.

The models underneath these agents are probabilistic. However good they get, they can be fooled into doing things they shouldn’t, and they can make mistakes. Telling an agent in its prompt what it mustn't do helps, but that's a request it won’t always honour. A control has to be enforced somewhere the agent can't change.

Isolation is the strongest of those controls, but every restriction makes the agent less useful, and people will work around tools that can't do the job. The key is giving each agent the access its task needs and no more. Visibility then shows whether you've drawn that line in the right place, and if (or where) you can safely loosen the reins.

Then there's the record of what an agent did. If it comes only from the agent, or from the harness running it (the framework the agent operates inside), it's only as reliable as the thing you're trying to oversee. The agent's own account is still worth having, because it shows what the agent set out to do. It just can't be the only record, because it's least reliable at the moment you need it most.

So oversight needs two things outside the agent and its harness: a view of what actually happened on the system, and the ability to stop the agent and roll back when something looks wrong. Neither should depend on the agent cooperating.

It helps to think about agents the way security teams think about people with privileged access. Insider threat programmes have long relied on observed behaviour over self-reporting, and the same principle applies to agents. Watch what the agent did, not what it says it did.

Saying yes to more agents

Done well, this lets an organisation approve more agents. Most organisations I talk to want to allow a wider range of agents, connected to more data sources, doing useful work. What usually holds them back is the worry that nobody would notice if an agent went somewhere or did something it shouldn't. Good visibility and effective guardrails deal with that worry, and once they're in place you can go faster.

Take a coding agent that needs to read from a production database to debug an issue. Without controls, the safe answer is no. With a read-only role for that task, no access to anything else and a log of every query it runs, you can approve it.

Visibility also changes the role security plays. I don't think security should have the final yes or no on which AI tools an organisation uses. A security team will naturally optimize for good security outcomes, sometimes at the expense of what the business is trying to do. The decision belongs with the data and AI function, or with a Chief AI Officer if you have one. Where neither exists yet, it sits best with whoever owns the AI adoption programme, often the CIO or CTO.

Of course, security should be a clear voice at the table alongside the other stakeholders, and once a tool is approved, security still owns its guardrails.

That voice simply carries more weight when it comes with evidence. Having an independent view of what agents are actually doing lets security tell the business, with some confidence, how far it's safe to go. And that’s a more useful role for security than being the final gate.

Before approving your next agent

Nobody I've spoken to has a complete answer yet to what replaces accountability for an agent. The closest I've found is a record of what the agent actually did, tied to the person who set it running, that the agent itself can't alter. Before approving your next agent, I'd challenge you to answer these questions:

Do you know which agents and tools are in use across your organisation, including the ones nobody approved?

Who has the final say on the next agent, and what does security need to show them to inform that call?

Could you stop an agent mid-action without relying on it to cooperate?

If an agent did something it shouldn't tomorrow, could you reconstruct what happened without relying on its own account?

I'll be working through these questions with Richard Smith, Founder of Codification and Alessandro Lo Prete from Sysdig's Threat Research Team on the panel at Ground Truth: London on 9 December. If these questions are on your list too, come and join us.

articles.title: NGINX2Root: Five RCE bugs in NGINX, a Linux kernel path to root, and how to detect exploitation
articles.context: The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) reviewed the disclosures and tested post-exploitation activity in a lab to help defenders understand who is exposed, what they can do...
articles.full_text:
On November 18, 2026, F5 published CVE records for five memory-safety bugs in NGINX, and the project shipped fixes the same day in NGINX 1.31.9 (mainline) and 1.30.7 (stable). Each bug allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to corrupt memory in an NGINX worker process, and all five carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2.

Xint, one of the teams that reported the bugs, published a write-up dubbing the set of vulnerabilities “NGINX2Root.” Xint also chained one of the NGINX bugs with a previously unknown Linux kernel bug in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) to get root on the host, including from inside a Docker container running the official NGINX image.

At the time of publication for this blog, there has been no public proof-of-concept (PoC) or reported in-the-wild exploitation. However, several teams found the HTTP/2 bugs independently, and both Xint and Wiz researchers say they’ve built working exploits that bypass address space layout randomization (ASLR). Also, the Linux kernel bug has not yet been assigned a CVE, nor has a fix been released.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) reviewed the disclosures and tested post-exploitation activity in a lab to help defenders understand who is exposed, what they can do before a fixed package reaches every host, and what runtime detection can see. This blog covers the five NGINX bugs, the kernel half of the chain, and what defenders can do now.

Timeline

All dates are in UTC.

Date

Event

Oct. 11

Xint finds the vulnerabilities.

Oct. 16

Xint reports them to F5 through HackerOne.

Oct. 21

Wiz Research reports confirmed remote code execution (RCE), with an ASLR bypass, for CVE-2026-123633 to F5.

Oct. 27

Xint's reports reach the NGINX development team.

Nov. 10

Xint finishes validating the patches.

Nov. 18

F5 publishes the five CVE records, NGINX 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 are released, and Xint and Wiz publish their research.

Nov. 18

Debian and Ubuntu list every supported release as vulnerable, with no fixed package yet.

The vulnerabilities and affected NGINX versions

CVE

Component

Reachable when

NGINX rating

Vulnerable (NGINX Open Source)

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 flow control: integer underflow leading to a heap buffer overflow

HTTP/2 is enabled

Major

1.9.5 – 1.31.8

CVE-2026-123633

HTTP/2 use-after-free

HTTP/2 is enabled, requests are proxied to an upstream, and the worker is low on worker_connections

Medium

1.19.7 – 1.31.8

CVE-2026-123634

Resolver use-after-free

The proxied server name uses variables, and an SSI or mirror subrequest resolves the same name

Medium

0.6.18 – 1.31.8

CVE-2026-121810

HTTP/3 use-after-free

HTTP/3 (QUIC) is enabled and requests are proxied to an upstream

Medium

1.25.0 – 1.31.8

CVE-2026-113425

Mail proxy use-after-free

The mail proxy runs with proxy on and auth_http

Major

0.5.33 – 1.31.8

All five CVE records have been assigned the same scores: 8.1 (High) on CVSS 3.1 and 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. NGINX2Root is network-based, doesn’t require authentication, and is relatively complex. F5 describes the impact as a worker crash or memory corruption, with code execution where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed. All five are data-plane bugs, and F5 states there is no control-plane exposure.

The fixed releases are NGINX 1.31.9 and 1.30.7. For NGINX Plus, they are 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 (37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1 fix CVE-2026-123633). The same release fixes five more NGINX CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a client request body over TLS 1.3, which NGINX rates as major. Upgrading to these versions fixes all 10 bugs.

Any NGINX version before 1.31.9 (mainline) or 1.30.7 (stable) is vulnerable if it has one of the features in the vulnerability table above enabled. How you check depends on where your NGINX comes from. There are four factors to consider for exposure:

Distribution packages: Distribution packages keep their version string when they backport a fix, so nginx -v won’t tell you whether you're patched. Ubuntu 24.04 ships NGINX 1.24.0, Ubuntu 22.04 ships 1.18.0, Debian 12 ships 1.22.1 and Debian 13 ships 1.26.3. Fixes for these will arrive as new package revisions. For example, Xint notes that Ubuntu 22.04's package went from 1.18.0-6ubuntu14 to 1.18.0-6ubuntu14.22 while still reporting 1.18.0. As of November 18, Debian and Ubuntu list every supported release as vulnerable to CVE-2026-123007, with no fixed package yet. NGINX.org packages, official images, and source builds report the upstream version, so nginx -v will provide an accurate patch status. The official nginx:1.31.9 image is available.

Container images: Images are only fixed when they are rebuilt on a fixed NGINX and redeployed. A running container doesn't change when the host is patched. Patch and redeploy.

Kubernetes ingress-nginx: The project was archived on March 24, 2026. Its README says there will be "no further releases, no bugfixes, and no updates to resolve any security vulnerabilities." The controller image includes its own NGINX build, so the project will not ship these fixes.

NGINX-derived software: Software built on NGINX's code, such as OpenResty, Tengine and Angie, is not named in the advisories. Check with those maintainers for possible exposure.

For scale, Xint counted 56.7 million hosts in Shodan identified as NGINX on November 10, 2026. Of the 11.94 million hosts that reported a version, 98.9% fell inside the 1.9.5 – 1.31.8 range vulnerable to CVE-2026-123007. Because of backports and feature requirements, a version banner doesn't prove a host is vulnerable. However, it does show how few public servers are on a current release.

Why teams should prioritize CVE-2026-123007

This is the bug with the widest reach. It needs only HTTP/2, which is a common setting on public HTTPS servers. Researchers have reported that serving ordinary static files is enough to reach the vulnerable code: No backend application or third-party module is needed. They have also confirmed RCE with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, over HTTP/2 with TLS on 64-bit systems. For example, Xint ran its exploit against a public HTTPS endpoint on AWS. The flaw itself dates back to NGINX 1.9.5, the release that added HTTP/2 support.

F5 credits four independent reporters for this CVE, and researchers describe exploitation as difficult. However, when four teams find the same bug independently, regardless of how challenging exploitation is, it is reasonable for defenders to assume that they’re not the only ones looking.

Understanding the other four NGINX2Root CVEs

Each of the other bugs requires a specific feature to be turned on, which narrows the potential list of exposed users:

CVE-2026-123633 also needs HTTP/2, plus proxying to an upstream. Turning off HTTP/2 blocks both HTTP/2 bugs.

CVE-2026-123634 needs a proxy_pass destination built from request variables, a resolver, and a subrequest from mirror or SSI. Researchers note that turning off mirror alone is not enough, because SSI also creates subrequests. Setting mirror_request_body on does not fix it either.

CVE-2026-121810 affects only servers with HTTP/3 enabled.

CVE-2026-113425 affects only servers that run the NGINX mail proxy with auth_http.

SCTP and the Linux kernel bug

The "to root" part of NGINX2Root is a separate bug. Researchers found a use-after-free and double-free in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, introduced by Linux 4.15 in 2018. According to Xint, it leaks kernel memory to defeat kernel ASLR and lets an attacker call an arbitrary kernel function. This bug currently has no CVE or patch, and researchers are withholding further details until a fix exists.

It’s important to note that hosts that never use SCTP are exposed, too. On most distributions, the sctp kernel module is not loaded until a process opens an SCTP socket, and then the kernel loads it automatically. So an attacker running code as an unprivileged NGINX worker can load the vulnerable code into the kernel themselves. In the Sysdig TRT lab, a single SCTP socket opened from the NGINX worker was enough to load sctp.ko. Once loaded, the module stays loaded until the next reboot.

Containers don't change this, because they share the host's kernel. Researchers ran the chain from inside a Docker container built from the official nginx:1.31.8 image and got root on the underlying host.

Blocking the module closes this path on hosts that don't need SCTP. With install sctp /bin/false in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/, the NGINX worker's SCTP socket call failed with EPROTONOSUPPORT in the Sysdig TRT lab, and the module was not loaded.

The block has three limits, however: It doesn't unload a module that is already loaded, it doesn't help where SCTP is compiled into the kernel, and it breaks workloads that use SCTP, such as telecom signaling and some Kubernetes network plugins.

The impact of NGINX2Root

Worker crashes and memory corruption: F5 describes the impact as a worker crash or memory corruption. An attacker can send crafted traffic to an exposed NGINX server without credentials.

Code execution as the NGINX worker: Researchers report working exploits that bypass ASLR. Normally, code execution in an NGINX worker is limited to the worker's unprivileged user.

Root on the host and container escape: The SCTP kernel bug turns a worker compromise into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container, because containers share the host's kernel.

A patch gap: The fix is released, but most fleets haven't received it yet. Most NGINX in production comes from a distribution package or a container base image. For those, the fix arrives when the distribution ships a backport and the image is rebuilt. Expect a gap of days or more between the upstream release and the build you actually run.

What this means for defenders

The fix is released, but most fleets haven't received it yet. Most NGINX in production comes from a distribution package or a container base image. For those, the fix arrives when the distribution ships a backport and the image is rebuilt. Expect a gap of days or more between the upstream release and the build you actually run.

The configuration workarounds are narrow and effective. Turning off HTTP/2 blocks the two most reachable bugs, including CVE-2026-123007. The other three need features that many deployments don't use. Find out which features your servers actually have enabled, so you know how much exposure you have before a fixed package arrives.

The kernel bug makes a worker compromise much worse. Normally, code execution in an NGINX worker is limited to the worker's unprivileged user. The SCTP bug turns that into root on the host, and an escape from the container. Blocking the sctp module costs nothing on hosts that don't use it. Today, this is the only mitigation for the kernel half of the chain.

Reloading isn't enough. A configuration reload leaves existing connections on the old worker processes. After you upgrade or change the configuration, restart NGINX, or confirm that every old worker has exited.

How to detect NGINX2Root

No public exploit code has been released and there is no reported in-the-wild exploitation, so the attack itself can't yet be replayed. Instead, the Sysdig TRT ran post-exploitation payloads from inside a real, vulnerable NGINX 1.31.8 worker process, in a container and on the host, which are the steps an attacker would take after gaining code execution.

However, researchers have confirmed RCE with an ASLR bypass, ran an exploit against a public HTTPS endpoint on AWS, and chained an NGINX bug with the SCTP kernel bug to get root on the host. These exploits have been described as difficult, but they are possible. Four teams found the CVE-2026-123007 vulnerability independently, so defenders should assume threat actors are working on it as well.

Threat intelligence

Sysdig Secure customers can use the Sysdig Threat Intelligence feed to find hosts and workloads that run an affected NGINX version, including NGINX bundled in other software. The feed checks versions, not enabled features. A host fixed by a distribution backport can stay listed until the feed is updated.

Runtime detection

Sysdig Secure customers can also detect attacker activity at each of these stages:

A shell started by the NGINX worker: Run shell untrusted.

A reverse shell from the worker: Reverse Shell Detected, and Redirect STDOUT/STDIN to Network Connection in Container.

A second-stage binary dropped and run: Drop and execute new binary in container, and Execution from /tmp.

Ordinary NGINX activity did not trigger any of these rules in our testing. This includes plain requests, HTTP/2 load, proxying, resolver and mirror traffic, configuration reloads, and the fixed NGINX 1.31.9 image.

Security teams should expect some alerts on patch day, because legitimate maintenance can resemble post-exploitation activity in some cases. For example, when we upgraded NGINX in place with its live binary upgrade (rather than a restart) in our lab, this triggered Sysdig Secure’s Non sudo setuid and Container Run as Root User rules. A configuration reload didn’t trigger these rules. If you upgrade this way, you’ll likely see similar alerts from your runtime detection tool. Scope any tuning to the maintenance window instead of suppressing the rules permanently to reduce the noise.

Researchers also suggest watching for these signs, though they note that these are general warning signs to be weighed together, and not confirmed indicators of vulnerability exploitation:

NGINX worker crashes and segmentation faults in error.log or coredumpctl.

Commands run by the NGINX worker's user.

Long-lived HTTP/2 connections that receive a large amount of data and send back very little.

Detecting NGINX2Root with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP requests. It can't see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. Use the Falco open source ruleset to detect post-exploitation activity such as a shell or a new binary started by an NGINX worker.

Recommendations

Patch

Upgrade to NGINX 1.31.9 or 1.30.7, or NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 or 37.0.8.1. Then, restart NGINX rather than reloading it, and confirm that every old worker process has exited.

Follow your distribution's advisory, not the upstream version number. Install the fixed package revision when it ships.

Rebuild and redeploy container images that include NGINX once a fixed base image is available.

Plan a migration off ingress-nginx. The project will not ship these fixes.

Temporary mitigation if you can’t patch right away

Disable HTTP/2 until you're patched. On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from listen. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from listen. Turn it back on after upgrading.

Remove request-time DNS lookups. Point proxy_pass at a fixed upstream group rather than a variable, and turn off mirror and SSI where you don't need them.

Disable HTTP/3. Remove quic listeners, set http3 off;, send Alt-Svc 'clear', and block UDP on the port.

Contain the blast radius, investigate, and audit

Block the SCTP module on hosts and Kubernetes nodes that don't use SCTP: add install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/. Run lsmod | grep sctp to check whether it's already loaded. If it is and nothing on the host uses it, the block takes effect after the next reboot.

Restrict the mail proxy. Bind the IMAP, POP3, and SMTP listeners to loopback, or allow only trusted sources through the firewall.

Watch for NGINX worker crashes and for processes started by NGINX workers.

Conclusion

NGINX2Root combines five NGINX bugs that already have a fix with one Linux kernel bug that doesn't.

The NGINX half is a patch-management problem: The upstream fix is out, but distribution packages and container images will take time to catch up, and the configuration workarounds can cover that gap. The kernel half requires immediate attention, and turns the compromise of an unprivileged worker into root on the host.

Although no public exploit has been released as of this blog’s publication, researchers already claim to have working POCs. The time for teams to patch is now.

If you use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Auto Mode, you benefit from AWS-managed infrastructure, but you still need runtime security for your workloads. Amazon EKS Auto Mode lets AWS run your Kubernetes cluster infrastructure: compute, networking, storage, load balancing, and node patching. That removes a lot of toil. Because AWS operates the nodes for you in a managed model, nodes are identical, predictable, and immutable, with read-only root filesystems and strict security controls. This post covers what that means for runtime security, and how to deploy and use Sysdig Secure with EKS Auto Mode using Universal eBPF.

What changes with Amazon EKS Auto Mode

With standard EKS, AWS manages the control plane, and you manage the worker nodes. Auto Mode extends AWS's responsibility to the nodes and the core cluster capabilities:

Nodes are AWS-managed appliances: a locked-down, container-focused OS (Bottlerocket-based) with a read-only root filesystem and SELinux enforcement. Nodes are replaced regularly, so they never drift. See the Auto Mode documentation for the full list of managed components.

Shared responsibility still applies

AWS managesYou manage

AWS's security guidance for Auto Mode and best practices cover the AWS side. This post covers the last row: what happens inside your workloads at runtime.

Why Auto Mode needs a different agent approach

Auto Mode nodes don't allow kernel module loading for security reasons. Because Bottlerocket fully supports eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter), Sysdig uses eBPF as the primary mechanism for runtime security. A Universal eBPF driver embedded in the Sysdig Host Shield (agent) enables a real-time approach to monitoring system activity safely within the kernel using system calls as a source of truth.

Learn more about kernel-level security monitoring.

How to get started

Sysdig deploys as a Kubernetes workload, so it follows Auto Mode nodes as AWS adds and replaces them. Nothing runs on the host outside Kubernetes.

Where Sysdig complements AWS-native controls

Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, EKS control-plane logging, network policies, and Pod Security Standards are recommended in an Auto Mode design. They cover the AWS and control-plane layers. Sysdig complements these controls with in-depth cloud workload protection. With Sysdig, security teams can apply runtime policies, investigate process activity, monitor file and workload behavior, and correlate events with Kubernetes context.

Customizable detection rules are built on the industry-leading Falco engine. It allows you to monitor system calls to identify errant or suspicious events at the Linux kernel level. You can use the default threat detection rules in Sysdig Secure or easily customize rules to work with your unique threat model.

The dynamic, short-lived nature of container workloads in a Kubernetes environment means static scanning and other traditional security measures may not detect threats that emerge at runtime. You need runtime security-the ability to monitor behavior in real time to quickly identify and address security issues for workloads running on Amazon EKS Auto Mode. For example, a compromised container might spawn an unexpected process or open a network connection that no vulnerability scanner would flag in advance. Runtime monitoring catches that behavior as it happens, with full Kubernetes context such as cluster, namespace, and workload identity.

We recommend proper posture management, including thorough container vulnerability scanning. Runtime security adds an extra layer of defense against exploits that static analysis or vulnerability scanners may miss, such as zero-days. Runtime security matters for modern organizations because it helps protect workloads and data from unauthorized access, malicious or unintentional changes, and suspicious behavior that could indicate an attack.

Try Amazon EKS Auto Mode with Sysdig

The fastest proof of value is a small EKS Auto Mode cluster with Sysdig on Universal eBPF. Check that core detections and Kubernetes context work, then test the response and investigation workflows that matter to your team. Ready to get started? You can request a demo, check out the installation docs, or read more about Sysdig for Kubernetes here: Runtime-Driven Security for Containers & Kubernetes — A Practitioner’s Toolkit.

articles.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Pre-auth RCE in OpenJDK, and the challenge of image and feature bloat
articles.context: Calif, the firm that discovered the vulnerability, says that with 64 A characters and one =, a remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, leak it Heartbleed-...
articles.full_text:
DISCLAIMER: This blog reflects public findings as of 1:36 UTC, Nov. 18, 2026, and it will be updated as new information is released.

Java promised that users would never have to think about memory again. Java's Base64 decoder, however, had other plans.

On November 17, 2026, Oracle and OpenJDK shipped fixes for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a heap memory corruption bug in the AVX-512 accelerated Base64 decoder. Calif, the firm that discovered the vulnerability, says that with 64 A characters and one =, a remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, leak it Heartbleed-style, and in the products they tested, get remote code execution (RCE).

Calif made a suggestion that Java4Shell’s Base64 optimization and the Squidbleed flaw that they also discovered are calls for vibe-uncoding, or the use of AI to find and remove system bloat to reduce an attack surface. This is the same point that’s been made in multiple Sysdig Cloud Native Security and Usage Reports since 2023 with regard to image bloat.

Let’s explore what's confirmed, what's still theoretical, and why after combating and cleaning up image bloat for years, the next fight appears to be feature bloat.

Important facts to know now about Java4Shell

What: Heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. Pre-authentication on common login paths.

Who: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (17, 21, 25, 27) on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. ARM is out. Java 11 and standard Java 8 are out. Oracle also lists the Java 8 performance build (8u511b33-perf) as vulnerable.

Severity: 9.2 critical on CVSS 4.0 per Calif, and 8.1 on CVSS 3.1 per OpenJDK's advisory.

Exploitation: Calif confirms working RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate without authorization, plus five more post-auth. The researcher says OpenAI Codex helped find the bug in an hour and build an exploit in two hours for less than $200. Calif stated the exploit will not be publicly shared until organizations have patched the vulnerability.

Fix: Oracle builds ending in .1, or -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as the bridge.

What happened

Time

Event

Nov 12

Oracle's pre-release notice: 11 Java SE fixes, all remotely exploitable without authentication, max CVSS 3.1 of 8.1. No CVE IDs.

Nov 17

Calif says the bug leaked ahead of the patch and moves its disclosure to 1 p.m. PT (21:00). Confirmed discussions about the report appear on X as early as 10:22.

Nov 17, 17:44 UTC

OpenJDK's advisory lists CVE-2026-114938 as hotspot/compiler, affecting 17, 21, 25, and 27.

Nov 17, 17:53 UTC

CISA KEV catalog is released. CVE not included.

Nov 17, 20:00 UTC

A lab reproduction of the overflow is published and says RCE isn't proven.

Nov 17, 21:00 UTC

Calif publishes its write-up, with RCE demos across named products.

Who's affected by Java4Shell

Calif's list of vulnerable builds is broad because everything downstream of OpenJDK inherits the code: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE, and Oracle GraalVM for JDK.

Line

Vulnerable (Oracle Java SE)

Fixed (Oracle)

Java 8 performance build

8u511b33-perf

8u513

Java 17

17.0.21.0.3

17.0.21.1

Java 21

21.0.13.0.3

21.0.13.1

Java 25

25.0.5.0.3

25.0.5.1

Java 27

27.0.1.0.3

27.0.1.1

For non-Oracle distributions, researchers said the Temurin, Corretto, and Zulu fixes were still pending at 20:00 UTC. To determine if your organization is affected, check with your vendor.

The hardware filter may be a silver lining for some organizations. The vulnerable code only runs on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. Use Calif's check to see if your Linux hosts are vulnerable:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

All four flags must show up. Then run java -version inside the container, not on the host. Your host's JDK is not your container's JDK, and your container's JDK is the one that matters.

How Java4Shell works

Per Calif's write-up, HotSpot's C2 compiler uses AVX-512 intrinsics to decode Base64 fast. The hand-rolled assembly that handles the padded tail miscalculates the output length for certain inputs, ending up with -1, which turns the write mask fully open. The result is that 64 bytes get written where two were expected, and 62 of them land past the end of the output array. Java then notices the input is bad and throws an exception, but the write already happened.

The trigger is 64 A characters followed by = (128 A plus = on Java 17). The decoder has to be JIT-compiled first, which means warm-up traffic. The overflowing bytes are fixed, so an attacker picks where the write lands, not what it writes.

That sounded like a dead end to some researchers, whose lab tests found that a typical token wasn’t able to corrupt anything, leading them to the early assumption that RCE was yet to be proven, but not impossible. However, Calif found the way around it: a classic heap grooming move borrowed from JavaScript engine exploitation. Use the fixed write to overwrite a neighboring array's length, and now you have a buffer that accepts chosen bytes. Do it again to get a reader; writer plus reader gives you a heap leak and a path to code execution.

What's reachable before login

Researchers found that standard Basic auth handling in Spring Security, Tomcat, and Jetty 12 passes the raw token to Base64.getDecoder() before validating it. Auth0's java-jwt decodes JWT headers and payloads the same way before checking the signature.

Calif adds that ordinary features like file uploads can expose the decoder too, and that samczsun contributed a client-side exploit: A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised even if it exposes no service. Ultimately, that means that your login page is likely the attack surface.

What's been demonstrated vs. what’s been claimed

Demonstrated by researchers:

Calif reports RCE in default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate (pre-auth), and Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker (post-auth). It also reports RCE in sample Struts and Spring Boot applications and publishes a demo video.

Theori and other firms have independently reproduced the overflow itself.

Calif says discovery took one hour, the first working exploit took two more, and the total token cost was under $200.

Constraints:

There is no universal exploit. Each target needs its own profile: a decoder route, a live writer, a feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action.

Wrong heap placement can crash the JVM. Calif says in many cases it can just retry.

The attack is sensitive to network latency. Calif's fix for that was renting a VM in the same region as the target.

Some chains need partial request bodies to reach the application. Request buffering (which nginx does by default) breaks those chains but isn't a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from a single complete request, and WebSocket tunnels bypass buffering.

What's public so far:

Calif published a self-contained Java program that warms the decoder and reproduces the 62-byte overwrite inside a bounded array.

Calif says it is holding back the weaponized, product-specific chains "until everyone has had a chance to upgrade," and will publish them later.

As of 21:10 UTC, GitHub repositories for the CVE ID were a placeholder README, Theori's mitigation tool, and a BigFix scanner. No exploit code. A search for java4shell exploit returned nothing. So far, researchers have shared a public trigger, a documented technique, named targets, and a promise of more to come. Leaked bugs often attract fake exploits, as researchers have already warned. So if a repo promises a shell, read it before you run it, and run it in a sandbox.

Reigning in image bloat

Calif closes its write-up with what it calls vibe-uncoding: If you don't need something, stop running it. They explicitly point to Base64 optimization as an example. It helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data and ships to everyone else too, and so "an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk."

As a cybersecurity strategist, this is a soapbox I’ve been on for about three years. Our annual cloud-native security and usage reports have continually made the same case: The unused packages that ride along with open source images do nothing for your use case and everything for an attacker's. The 2025 report specifically called for shrinking image bloat through consolidation, smart application building, and discovering shadow AI and other shadow IT.

And then organizations actually did it, and I’d like to think they used AI to do so, just as Calif suggests. In the 2026 Cloud-Native Security and Usage Report, we analyzed nearly 13 billion packages for image bloat. Less than one percent of packages in images were unused, a 50% reduction year over year. Teams matured their CI/CD pipelines and moved to leaner images, which in turn shrinks the attack surface. And, as a bonus, it makes images build, scan, and pull faster and cost less to store. Fewer packages means fewer surprises, faster patching, and clearer ownership.

That’s a win. Image bloat will probably never hit 0%, but it’s a material reduction that came from boring, disciplined work.

Here's the catch, and the real lesson of Java4Shell: The cleanup got the unused packages, but it didn't touch the unused code inside the packages you do use. Nobody's image scan flags a hand-rolled AVX-512 Base64 stub sitting inside java.base, because Java is in use, Base64 is in use, and the optimization is part of the thing. Package-level bloat is mostly handled. Feature-level bloat is the next frontier, and it lives upstream, in runtimes and libraries that ship everything to everybody.

Calif's answer is to point AI at that problem too: Find the dead code and needless optimizations, then remove them. I think this question of "What can we delete?" is the right one, aimed one layer deeper than most of us have been looking.

But slimming your images will not stop this specific bug. The vulnerable code is in the JDK itself, in the thing you actually use. Two things do apply, however:

The flag is vibe-uncoding at runtime. -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics turns off a feature you probably didn't need. That mitigation works because most workloads never notice.

Blast radius is a real control. If an attacker lands code execution in a minimal image with no shell, no package manager, no curl, and no compiler, they have a much worse afternoon than in an image with everything. Leftover tooling doesn't cause the bug, but it's the toolkit the attacker finds afterward.

And there’s another important lesson CISOs can learn from this: Calif's researcher found this by prompting Codex over an audit of the JIT compiler, intrinsics, and crypto and in the researcher's own words, "ignoring slops for around 20 minutes." Discovery to working exploit in three hours. That’s the new math for defenders. If your patch cycle is measured in weeks and the other side's exploit cycle is measured in an afternoon, you’ve lost the race.

That is the same theme running through our 2026 report and other Sysdig threat research identified throughout the year: shifting from manual effort to machine-speed defense, with runtime detection as the signal teams trust most.

How to detect Java4Shell

This exploit leaves almost nothing at the application layer. The server answers 401 and moves on. Defenders should look for the shape, noise, and aftermath of an attack.

Request shape: Flag Base64-alphabet tokens of 32 or more characters that end in = and whose length isn't a multiple of 4. Valid padded Base64 is always a multiple of 4. Start with Authorization headers.

Application logs: Researchers saw IllegalArgumentException: Input byte array has wrong 4-byte ending unit on every attempt in their tests.

Retry and warm-up behavior: Calif's chain warms the decoder with valid decodes, then triggers, and retries on bad placement. That implies bursts of requests from one source, repeated malformed tokens, and potentially many half-sent request bodies held open and released together. However, this has not been observed in the wild as of this publication.

JVM crashes: Wrong placement means crashes: SIGSEGV, hs_err_pid*.log files, and bursts of worker restarts.

Post-exploitation: If the chain lands, the aftermath looks like any other Java compromise: the JVM spawning a shell, dropping and executing a binary, or opening connections it never opened before.

What defenders can do to get ahead of Java4shell today

Patch Oracle JDK immediately. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1, and 8u513 for the performance build.

Linux users don’t have to self-patch: Java installed from your Linux distribution's package manager gets fixed through the distribution's normal update channel, but only after the distro ships a fix and only on hosts that apply updates. Containers and vendor JDK builds don’t update themselves. Rebuild and redeploy.

Inventory everything else. Check Temurin, Corretto, Zulu, Microsoft, and distribution builds against your vendor's advisory. Several were pending as of this publication.

Prioritize by exposure and hardware. Internet-facing services on AVX-512 VBMI instances, especially anything using Basic auth, java-jwt, or the products on Calif's list, go first.

Mitigate with a JVM flag if you can’t patch yet. -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics stopped the overflow on every affected version Upwind tested. -XX:UseAVX=2 also works but turns off all AVX-512 paths and fails to start on ARM hosts, so apply it to x86-64 only. Both need a restart.

Make sure you use the right flag, or you may break something. -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock fails without -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions. Pushed fleet-wide through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, that's an outage you caused yourself.

Think hard before running someone's runtime patch. Some proposed tools attach an agent to live JVMs without a restart, distributed via curl | sh with pinned certificates and hash checks, which attaches code to production. Read it, test it, schedule it, and expect a temporary throughput dip.

Hunt backward. Search Authorization headers and application logs for the shapes above, and check for hs_err_pid files and unexplained restarts since before today.

Keep deleting, and go a layer deeper. Unused packages are down to under one percent of what's in images, so keep that discipline. Then ask what feature, shell, or optimization you could turn off inside the things you do use.

Conclusion

Java4Shell is the third entry in a pattern defenders should have memorized by now: a widely deployed platform, a bug in the low-level code underneath the safe layer, and a researcher with an AI assistant who went from audit to exploit in a few hours. The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) has been tracking the same theme across vulnerabilities like PHP2Shell, Node2Shell, and the Apache HTTP Server mod_http2 bug. The names may change (slightly), but the story remains familiar.

The next iteration may look like a library or runtime a team forgot was in its stack, hit through a field they didn’t know was parsed before auth. The defenses that hold up are the basic ones we know all too well: Know what you run, patch what's exposed first, run less of what you don’t need, and watch what it does at runtime so you aren't relying on the exploit having the courtesy to announce itself early.

Memory safety comes with an asterisk that is often written in assembly. Teams have cleaned up the packages, and now it’s time to pare down the features.

Check out the latest in threat research from the Sysdig TRT

articles.title: HTTPd (CVE-2026-119618): Detecting heap corruption and RCE in Apache HTTP Server mod_http2
articles.context: Threat Intelligence entries show where affected Apache hosts are running, Vulnerability Management maps to each distribution’s vendor advisory, and Runtime Detections catch what...
articles.full_text:
On November 11, 2026, Apache released HTTP Server 2.4.71 to fix CVE-2026-119618, a critical severity heap corruption flaw in mod_http2 that Apache’s security advisory said can lead to remote code execution (RCE). The flaw sits in assign_headers(), affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and can be triggered over HTTP/2 with no authentication. Red Hat and Amazon have scored the vulnerability 9.8 on CVSS v3.1, though CISA rates it at 8.1.

Two teams found the bug independently, eight days apart. Anthropic's OSS Scanner is an opt-in, model-driven scanner for open-source projects. It reported the bug on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it eight days later on November 3, according to the CVE record.

The day after Apache disclosed it on oss-security, a public proof-of-concept (PoC) was published on GitHub showing the heap corruption, though no PoC has been released for the RCE as of the publication of this blog. Additionally, no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported, and the CVE does not appear in CISA's KEV catalog.

The bug lives in Apache's own HTTP/2 implementation, not in any application the server hosts. Only servers that enable HTTP/2 are exposed. Affected organizations are encouraged to upgrade to version 2.4.71 or turn off HTTP/2 if patching is delayed.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed the publicly available research and simulated a successful exploit to help defenders understand four key details: who is affected, what has been demonstrated versus claimed, what runtime visibility can detect, and what mitigation steps should be taken until a patch can be applied. They also tested and found that Sysdig’s existing runtime detections caught every post-exploitation step.

Timeline

Date

Event

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reports the flaw as ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ

Oct. 30, 2026

CVE ID reserved

A public PoC is posted on GitHub showing heap corruption

Affected Apache HTTP Server versions

The flaw is in mod_http2, the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server. The same module is released separately as mod_h2 on GitHub and also affected.

While the Apache advisory rates the vulnerability as critical. The CVE record, which Apache maintains as the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), doesn’t actually carry an associated CVSS score. However, Red Hat and Amazon both rate the vulnerability as critical and score it at 9.8 on CVSS v3.1 and CISA rates it as a high severity vulnerability at 8.1 on CVSS v3.1.

Red Hat rates its own RHEL 9 and 10 builds Important rather than Critical. Those builds allocate each HTTP/2 stream from "a separate allocator, which substantially increases the complexity of exploiting the flaw."

The severity and prioritization of this vulnerability in an organization’s environment depends first on whether HTTP/2 is on.

The version number alone won’t confirm exposure, check these additional factors:

Distribution packages: Vendors often backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so check your vendor's advisory and not only httpd -v or apache2 -v.

As of November 13, fixes are out for Debian 12 and 13 (2.4.71-1~deb12u1 and 2.4.71-1~deb13u1), Ubuntu 22.04 through 26.10, Alpine, Fedora, Amazon Linux 2 and 2023, and Wolfi and Chainguard.

SUSE, openSUSE, Photon OS, and several RHEL rebuilds were still waiting on vendor fixes.

Downstream products: Vendors that repackage httpd, such as Red Hat JBoss Core Services (jbcs-httpd24-mod_http2) and Red Hat Hardened Images, may be listed as affected on version number alone. Whether you are exposed depends on what the product ships. Check that mod_http2 is actually present and loaded. For example, Sysdig’s scan of the Red Hat Hardened Images httpd image shows it listed as affected, but the image has no mod_http2, so the risk can be accepted. Check the vendor’s advisory for fix status.

Recent upgrades: Servers upgraded to 2.4.67 for the HTTP/2 flaw in May, CVE-2026-23918, are still inside this CVE's affected range.

How the HTTPd RCE flaw works

HTTP/2 carries many requests over one connection as parallel streams and that concurrency is where this flaw lies.

The Apache advisory calls the flaw "Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization" in assign_headers(), and the CVE record lists CWE-362. Red Hat lists CWE-20 instead. Red Hat describes the root cause as "a worker thread writes into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared, lock-free allocator." In practice, two threads can corrupt the same heap.

The fix is a one-line change in assign_headers(). Before the fix, a request with a content type that had already ended had its zero Content-Length header written into the HTTP/2 request's own header table (req->headers). The fix writes it into the per-request table (r->headers_in) instead. The commit message gives no explanation. Red Hat's statement supplies the threading context.

What is reachable

Exposure depends on configuration. Red Hat states that only servers with HTTP/2 enabled through the Protocols directive are affected:

HTTP/1.1 only

According to RedHat, servers serving only HTTP/1.1 are not affected.

Red Hat's Bugzilla entry says an unauthenticated attacker triggers the flaw "by sending specially crafted HTTP/2 frames." That puts internet-facing, HTTP/2-enabled httpd in the first patch tier. This table does not cover reverse proxies in front of httpd.

HTTPd RCE exploitation: What's been demonstrated vs. claimed

According to Red Hat’s CVE page, public research has shown "a reliable exploit against a default-configured server." However, without a researcher name or links to details, this can’t be verified. As of the publishing of this blog, no other security researchers or vendors have confirmed exploitation.

As of about 16:00 UTC on November 12, a GitHub search for the CVE returned four repositories: a proof of concept, a patch-status tracker, and two detection or assessment tools.

The PoC reports heap corruption, not code execution. Its README describes the impact as "Heap corruption in an httpd child process; potential remote code execution."

Its evidence comes from a lab build:

Setup: httpd 2.4.70 built from upstream source on a debian:bookworm container, running the prefork MPM with Protocols h2c http/1.1.

Results: The PoC sent 6,080 requests. AddressSanitizer reported five crashes, including a heap use-after-free allocated in assign_headers(). ThreadSanitizer reported 31 allocator races.

Fixed build: A 2.4.71 build showed none.

Trigger: A request that ends without a body and carries a Content-Type but no Content-Length triggers the bug. The fix commit changes exactly that code path.

The README doesn't show control of the corrupted memory, and the author has published no exploit.

The bottom line is that unauthenticated HTTP/2 traffic can crash and corrupt the heap of a vulnerable httpd. Remote code execution is possible, but nobody has publicly demonstrated it yet. Treat the crash as likely wherever HTTP/2 is on, and code execution as a credible risk.

HTTPd RCE impact

Nothing publicly disclosed as of November 13, 2026, shows in-the-wild exploitation, a mass-scanning campaign, or a public RCE exploit. The primary sources do establish the following:

Risk of unauthenticated RCE: Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach the server could execute arbitrary commands with no authentication. Bugzilla adds that commands run as the httpd process.

Worker crashes: The public PoC crashes httpd child processes on a vulnerable build.

Long-lived exposure: The affected range starts at 2.4.55, so servers patched for earlier HTTP/2 bugs can still be exposed.

Paths with no fix yet: Standalone mod_h2 has no fixed release. Several distributions, including SUSE, openSUSE, Photon OS, and CentOS Stream 10, were still waiting on vendor fixes as of November 13.

Detecting HTTPd RCE with Sysdig Secure

Sysdig Secure customers have three layers of coverage for CVE-2026-119618. Threat Intelligence entries show where affected Apache hosts are running, Vulnerability Management maps to each distribution’s vendor advisory, and Runtime Detections catch what a successful exploit does once an attacker enters a vulnerable environment.

Threat intelligence

Sysdig Secure customers have two entries for CVE-2026-119618 in the Threat Intelligence feed. Each entry lists the affected hosts and running Kubernetes workloads. One entry uses the SBOM to find affected versions of Apache HTTP Server, mod_http2, and the vendor packages that contain the module. The other entry lists the assets where Sysdig Vulnerability Management reports the CVE.

Vulnerability management

Sysdig vulnerability management detects CVE-2026-119618 across your environment. To prioritize remediation, start with internet-facing workloads and packages in use at runtime.

Sysdig vulnerability scanning reports this CVE by distribution and release, and each status follows the vendor's own advisory.
