Runtime detection

The Sysdig TRT simulated a successful exploit inside a vulnerable Apache server, both inside a container and as a host service. Existing runtime threat detections caught every step without rule modifications, including:

Failed exploit attempts that crash web server workers

Commands or a shell started by the web server, including reverse shells

Tools downloaded and run by the web server

The web server process replaced by attacker code

A successful attack would give the attacker code execution as the httpd worker. From there, attackers do what they do after any web server RCE: open a reverse shell, download and run a tool, start a miner, steal cloud credentials, or try a kernel local privilege escalation.

Detecting HTTPd RCE with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP/2 frames. It cannot see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. That includes a shell or unexpected binary spawned by an httpd process, an unexpected outbound connection, or a write to a sensitive path.

Web servers fork helpers legitimately, so rules scoped to httpd need tuning to stay quiet. The post-exploitation strategies above apply.

Recommendations

Patch

Update httpd on every server: Move to 2.4.71, or to your vendor's patched package. On RHEL 9 that is mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1, on RHEL 10 mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1, and on Debian trixie apache2 2.4.71-1~deb13u1. Patching is the only complete fix.

Restart httpd and rebuild images after you patch: A running server keeps the old module loaded. Verify the package version inside the running workload.

Replace standalone mod_h2: The project is archived, and its latest release, 2.0.42, is affected.

Interim mitigations if you cannot patch today

Disable HTTP/2: Apache's advisory and oss-security notice give no workaround. Wiz recommends removing h2 and h2c so the setting reads Protocols http/1.1. That is Wiz's guidance, not Apache's. It matches Red Hat's statement that HTTP/1.1-only servers are not affected.

Apply the change server-wide and in every virtual host.

Restart or reload httpd so the change takes effect.

Test latency-sensitive services first. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1, which can slow multiplexed workloads.

Contain the blast radius

Run httpd workers as an unprivileged user: Limit what a compromised worker can read and write.

Keep secrets out of the server's reach: Use a secrets manager, not environment variables or files the worker can read.

Investigate and audit

Audit your environment: Find every host and workload running httpd 2.4.55–2.4.70 or mod_h2 2.0.8–2.0.42 with HTTP/2 enabled, internet-facing first. Sysdig Secure customers can use the Threat Intelligence entry and Vulnerability Management findings.

Watch for crashing httpd children: Repeated child-process segfaults on an HTTP/2-enabled server match what the public PoC produces.

Review httpd process activity: Look for shells, downloads or outbound connections from httpd workers since public disclosure on November 11.

Enable default runtime policies: Sysdig’s runtime detections will catch exploitation, even when a vulnerability scan has no findings yet.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-119618 is a threading bug in httpd's HTTP/2 module, not a flaw in the applications httpd serves. Heap corruption and crashes are public. Code execution is claimed but not yet publicly shown, but that gap is why reachability should drive patch prioritization. Defenders should start with HTTP/2-enabled, public-facing servers.

The timelines are still important to note for security teams. Two teams reported the bug independently, eight days apart. One “team" was an automated, model-driven scanner, while the other was a human team. By November 12, a day after disclosure, a public PoC that corrupts the heap was on GitHub. The window between “advisory published” and “working exploit” is small, and organizations need to be prepared to respond quickly to these notifications.

In this case, the best course of action is to patch first. Until every server is patched and restarted, disable HTTP/2 where you can and use runtime detection to close the gap. A runtime sensor will not see the heap corruption, but it will catch what a successful exploit does next.

articles.title: Refreshing the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Detection and Response in the AI era
articles.context: It used to take attackers days to conduct reconnaissance, lateral movement, and exploitation, but now it only requires a few minutes
articles.full_text:
How long does it take your security teams to detect a threat, correlate and contextualize relevant data, and take action? For most organizations, the honest answer is still measured in hours or days. Mature organizations are actively working toward reducing that time to minutes, and the most innovative teams are moving to sub-minute timescales using agentic AI.

The reality is that attackers don’t wait. Researchers across the industry, like the Sysdig Threat Research Team, have continuously shown that cloud attacks unfold in 10 minutes or less, and with AI and agentic workflows, the window for defense continues to shrink.

In mid-July 2026, Hugging Face disclosed a security incident unlike anything the industry had documented before. An agentic security research harness breached their production infrastructure. This harness was later confirmed to be part of OpenAI’s internal cyber-capability evaluation. Hugging Face logged more than 17,000 recorded events before the agents were contained, and they deployed LLM-driven analysis agents to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, and map the credentials touched. It took an AI to catch an AI.

Just one month prior, the Sysdig TRT documented JADEPUFFER, which targeted AI and ML infrastructure with purpose-built ransomware. The attacker was also an agent with no human at the keyboard.

These are not isolated incidents; they are the new normal. AI-assisted attacks have compressed the kill chain, and frontier AI models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos have uncovered thousands of new vulnerabilities, too. It used to take attackers days to conduct reconnaissance, lateral movement, and exploitation, but now it only requires a few minutes.

“Cloud threats aren’t just fast; they are automated. Without real-time visibility, an attacker can move from a container escape to resource hijacking in minutes, spiking your compute costs before your team even receives an alert. Early detection is the only way to intercept execution before it impacts your bottom line.” — CISO at a Cryptocurrency Exchange and Trading Platform

The 555 Benchmark was designed for this

The 555 Benchmark for Cloud Detection and Response gives organizations a framework to meet this reality: detect threats in 5 seconds, investigate them in 5 minutes, and respond with precision in 5 minutes. And with agentic capabilities in the hands of defenders, meeting that benchmark is more than achievable.

When 555 was first introduced, it was a challenge; something to work toward. The Hugging Face incident, and other reports of agentic threat actors (ATAs), make clear why this benchmark is now a business imperative. When an autonomous system can break out and breach a production infrastructure via the fastest path, our concern is no longer whether AI can find vulnerabilities. It is whether organizations have continuous visibility into what attackers can reach, what they did, and how quickly they can be stopped. That is exactly what 555 operationalizes.

Ultimately, the 555 Benchmark isn’t a product or quick fix to implement, but a call to action to pressure-test your security processes against the speed of modern attacks. By continuously improving and modernizing your people, processes, and tooling, and by supplementing them with well-governed agentic AI security capabilities, you can reduce the risk of material breach, reputational damage, and financial loss.

Long gone are the days of working to defend your environment over the course of several days. Today, you only have minutes to respond to an attack.

“I don't want to know 15 minutes after someone breached my system. I need to know instantly so we can shut it down before the blast radius expands. To move at the necessary speed, you need to not only be alerted to the right things, but also respond appropriately. Having a benchmark gives us a goal to hold ourselves to.” — Désiré Banse, Former NIST Researcher and Security Operations Manager at a healthcare technology company

Introducing the updated 555 Benchmark Guides for CISOs and practitioners

To help organizations operationalize this framework for the AI era, Sysdig has republished two guides — aimed at different roles working toward the same goal — to support and encourage organizations in striving for 10-minute threat detection and response.

One guide is designed for the practitioners who work in and around the SOC: the security professionals in the trenches and on the front lines. The Hugging Face response team is a model for what this looks like in practice: After the breach was contained, they used agentic AI to do in hours what would’ve taken a team of analysts days. This guide focuses on how to operate at machine speed using the automation, AI tooling, and agentic workflows that make 555 achievable.

“Cloud threat detection and response goes far beyond tooling. You need to implement a specific set of skills and finesse and a different kind of mindset to detect cloud attacks in real time. ”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners

The other guide is for the CISOs and security leaders who are responsible for leading teams through battle. They own the security strategy and risk, and must report value and breach impact to the board and to other business functions. This guide aligns security outcomes with organizational risk and reflects how, in the AI era, speed is the defining risk factor and defining board-level question.

“For large enterprises, a single hour of downtime costs over $100,000, with industries like finance, healthcare, media, and communications reaching well over $5 million per hour.”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs

Together, these guides provide a framework for security teams and leaders to meet common goals and expectations. It also helps them speak a unified language. By collaborating and following the strategies outlined, they can implement changes that modernize and accelerate cloud security practices, turning what were once ambitious goals into operational reality.

Enterprise security is like a symphony orchestra, with the CISO as the conductor. An oboist cannot sit in for a violinist, and different teams play their own distinct roles. SOC analysts, developers, platform engineers, and business stakeholders each contribute unique skills to the overall composition. Today, AI agents have joined that orchestra — not replacing whole sections, but playing alongside them, automating manual, repetitive processes and handling the parts that move too fast for humans hands alone, so humans can exercise judgment and have a greater impact. Synchronization and speed are survival requirements to maintain a secure and harmonious organization.

What you’ll learn

The updated 555 guides were designed to help organizations mature and modernize detection and response for the AI era through:

Collaboration: Working cross-functionally inside and outside of security and technical teams around shared context and outcomes to enable coordinated, real-time detection and response as humans and automated systems work together.

Integration: Unifying cloud-native telemetry and identity behaviors across cloud, SaaS, and AI systems to build real-time, decision-ready context across your entire environment to enable faster, more accurate detection and response.

Automation: Reducing manual effort across detection, investigation, and response to keep pace with AI-driven attacks by enabling orchestration to execute at machine speed.

Fast and automated incident response = Less attack risk = Lower chance of materiality = Business and operational value of security

If your organization operates in the cloud, now is the time to reassess how fast your security processes actually move. You don’t always need more tools or budget, but you do need the right architecture and better orchestration of the people, processes, and tooling you already have to modernize your cloud threat detection and response and meet the speed that threats demand.

Read and share The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs and The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners today. Attackers are already running at machine speed — it’s time your defense does, too.

articles.title: What one organization revealed about AI agent risk
articles.context: A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents With early access to Sysdig AI Defense, one software development company spent a month looking at AI agent usage across their enterprise
articles.full_text:
A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents

With early access to Sysdig AI Defense, one software development company spent a month looking at AI agent usage across their enterprise. Below is what they found.

Citizen developers are generating code

At this organization, 50% of the employees using AI agents work outside of the engineering department. Marketing, human resources, sales, legal, and finance all used AI agents daily, and they aren’t just chatting with them. Among the non-engineers using agents, an average of 42% of them had an agent run code, a build, a package install, or a cloud or cluster command.

A finance employee building tools likely doesn’t possess the same security knowledge as an engineer, nor are they likely to have the same reviews in place by default. But that shouldn’t stop them from creating. Organizations should watch installs and CLI calls and provide an approved, sandboxed path for them to build.

Tool calls are running without human approval

People turn off prompts to keep their work moving, and although it isn’t generally a sign of carelessness, it can open organizations up to greater risk. More than 60% of this organization’s tool calls ran without a human approving them — 52% screened by Claude Code’s auto-mode classifier instead of a person, and 9% with permission prompts intentionally turned off (YOLO mode).

But the answer to minimizing this risk isn’t blocking everything or turning a blind eye. Organizations need to understand their risk profiles at different levels, and allow tools, agents, and extensions based on what they can reach and change.

The agent’s account of its own actions isn’t enough

For every tool call this organization’s agents logged, the kernel captured seven processes. While an agent’s log may help a user debug a session, it’s not meant to be used as audit evidence because the agent writes it. The kernel sees what actually ran at the process level, regardless of the tool or API used. However, additional data shows that the security team needs both to see the full picture. For example, when an agent read a credential file, the agent’s log had no entry 82% of the time. However, the kernel logged every read.

Connecting unverified extensions to agents

Nearly half (47%) of the MCP servers in use came from third-party registries or vendors for this organization. Each server is a trusted relationship that only takes one line of config to connect to an agent, and once connected, it has access. Servers can also update silently in the background, so the one you trusted last week may not be the one running today.

Matching models to tasks

More than 50% of the organization’s AI spend went to duplicative processes and capabilities. With visibility into which models are used, scoped to the team and user behind each agent, organizations can tie model choice to the task and cut duplication.

What else is in the full report

This is only a fraction of what one month of agent activity uncovered. Dig deeper to discover:

How often security-relevant detections are triggered.

A risk-tier framework for allowing agents and extensions by what they can reach

Real alerts from the deployment, including a possible data exfiltration, an unapproved model provider, and a change to cloud permissions.

What model tiers employees are actually using day to day.

A risk reduction table you can hand to your team.

Odds are, AI agents are already running in your organization. The question is whether you know where they’re running, and whether you can see what they’re doing. Read the full report to see what this organization found and how you can start closing the gap.

articles.title: Introducing Sysdig AI Defense: See, stop, and prove what agents do
articles.context: Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research
articles.full_text:
AI has moved from assisting to acting. Agents now read files, run commands and reach your cloud with a real person’s access. Most of the time, the only record of what they did is the one the agent wrote itself. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” shows where one software company's agents logged one tool call for every seven processes the kernel actually watched them run. And it isn’t only engineers. Someone in finance can wire up a coding agent on a Tuesday afternoon. Every agent, model and seat they add becomes a line item most companies can’t trace to a team or a task.

Find every agent, decide what it can do, keep the record

Sysdig AI Defense is runtime security and governance for every AI agent your teams run, from the laptop where an agent starts its work to the cloud where its actions land.

It starts by showing you what’s there. It finds the agents, MCP servers, skills and plugins your people use, including the ones nobody approved, and ties each one to the account and the person behind it.

Then you decide what agents are allowed to do. Most of the time, nothing changes. Everything your policies don’t name runs as normal, so developers keep working. For the actions you care about, you pick the response. Confirm pauses the call and asks the developer to approve it first. Block refuses it outright. A kill process ends the work the moment the process starts.

Whatever happens, there’s a record. Every action Sysdig AI Defense sees lands in your Sysdig tenant, off the device, where the agent can’t change it. Security can prove what happened, and leaders can see which teams use which models for which work.

Under the hood, it’s the same runtime engine Sysdig built to protect cloud workloads. Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research. What’s new is where it looks. It now follows AI agents wherever they work.

By default, Sysdig AI Defense doesn't collect the prompts your people type or the agent's replies. File edits and tool results are removed before they leave the machine. Your data stays in your Sysdig tenant, in the region you choose.

See every agent and MCP server your teams run, then decide what they can use

The questions security leaders ask us most are simple: what agents are running, which ones has nobody approved, and who owns them? Most can't answer these questions yet. In a 2026 IBM study, 77% of organizations surveyed said AI adoption is already outpacing their governance, and two-thirds of the CIOs and CTOs said they are held accountable for AI systems they do not fully control. Sysdig AI Defense answers from what is actually running, across tools like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, and it follows agents across the whole AI fabric: employee workstations, production Linux and Kubernetes, and the managed agent platforms you don’t own.

Most security teams are likely running more agents than they know about. One software company with about 300 machines found that out in its first month on Sysdig AI Defense. Nothing was blocked, because every policy ran in Alert for the whole month. The full findings are in our “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents”. Half the agents Sysdig AI Defense found on those machines were instances the security team didn’t know about. Employees had signed up with personal email addresses on company devices, outside single sign-on, and every device had at least one agent harness installed and in active use.

Shadow AI isn’t only unapproved agents, either. Early adopters reported finding Ollama, llama.cpp and LM Studio running on people’s machines, a Qwen coding model served locally, and models downloaded straight to laptops. None of that crosses your AI gateway, so the gateway never sees it. The kernel does. It sees each one install, start and pull a model, and ties it to the person behind it.

Once you can see it, you can decide what’s allowed. New AI tools show up in the inventory as they appear on devices. If you don’t want agents using an MCP server, or one of its tools, deny it and set the policy to Block. The agent’s call is refused before it runs, and the agent sees your reason. If there’s a service agents should never send data to, name it in a policy, and kill process ends the upload as the process starts.

‍

Let agents work, and stop only the action that goes too far

An allowlist makes it easy to stop what you already know you don't want. The action itself is harder to judge, because it happens in the middle of a job, often in a fraction of a second. Even the labs that build these models have watched their own agents cross a line. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed cases where agents working through test tasks reached real systems that belonged to someone else. So the check has to happen at the moment the agent acts. Block and Confirm policies step in on the agent’s tool call before it runs. Kill process catches any process the moment it starts, no matter which agent launched it. You choose which response each policy gets.

Take a file of customer records. Opening one is ordinary work for an agent, and most of the time it is fine. What matters is where the data goes next, and what the agent gave itself permission to do along the way. A read that stays on the machine passes without a second look. The same read, followed by an upload to a public file-sharing host by an agent that just widened its own permissions, is an incident.

When an agent is told no, it tries another route, like a shell command or a script it writes itself. A hook sees the command but is blind to the script. AI Defense sees both. It sees the command with its destination parsed out, and the script as it starts.

You don’t have to write policy from scratch. Start from Sysdig’s managed policies for the risks agents bring, such as MCP servers and tools, secrets and data, and destructive commands. Each one is written as Falco rules you can read. You also don’t have to turn on blocking on day one. Every Sysdig policy starts in Alert, which means it raises what it sees and stops nothing. Watch what it catches on your own fleet. Then choose Block, Confirm or Kill process for the actions that matter. For actions you want a human on, Confirm sends the call to the agent’s own permission prompt, so the developer approves or refuses it right where they’re already working. Security decides which actions need that second look. Everything else runs as normal.

Not every risk fits a rule written in advance. Agents pick up new skills all the time. That’s why Sysdig’s threat research rules also look for agent behavior that resembles an attack, like credential dumping, persistence, tunnels and remote access.

Here’s what that looks like in our demo environment. A revenue operations agent, running with approvals turned off, tries to send a customer export to a public file host. A Kill process policy ends the upload as it starts, and the agent tells the person why.

When security wants to see how it got there, session replay steps through the session’s tool calls in order. The detections and kills show up in the Events rows beside it, each naming the rule and policy that fired.

See which model tier each team uses, for which task

Because every agent is tied to a person, so is every model it uses. Each session carries the model it ran on and the person and team behind it, whether or not the traffic goes through an AI gateway.

That matters for AI spend. In the same findings, four in ten employees ran Opus-class models only. Sysdig AI Defense rates each person’s model tier against how demanding their work was, by team. It flags light work running on the most expensive models, so leaders can change the habit before the invoice shows up. It also flags heavy work on the cheapest models, where someone may be stuck with a model too light for the job. Managers can move them to a better fit and help them get more done.

Answer an audit without pulling developers off their work

When an auditor asks what an agent did and who was behind it, most teams have one place to look, which is the agent’s own log. That log can miss a lot.

The kernel is the part of the operating system every action passes through, which makes it a good place to check. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” found that the agent’s own log had no entry for 82% of the credential-file reads the kernel recorded, and no entry for 95% of the reads the agent binary made itself. Across that month, the kernel recorded 2.6 million processes against 374,000 tool calls in the agents’ own logs. The agent’s log is useful context, but it leaves out too much to carry an audit on its own.

Sysdig AI Defense keeps its own record from the kernel, off the device, where the agent can't change it. Remove Sysdig AI Defense’s own hook and it puts it back within the hour, and the kernel keeps recording in between. Each event carries the agent, the account, the model and the session. Each detection names the rule and policy behind it. With Sysdig AI Defense, the evidence is already on file when an audit asks about AI, and nobody has to pull a developer off their work to rebuild it. Teams can also forward these records to their SIEM, where they sit with the rest of their security evidence.

Accountability for agents starts at runtime

Boards are asking what agents are doing, and regulators are starting to ask too. Hatem Naguib, Sysdig's CEO, has boiled it down to three questions every executive should be able to answer:

How do we know our AI isn't going rogue?

What AI are we using, and who is accountable for it?

What can we prove?

None of these can be answered from the agent's own log alone.

Falco has passed 200 million downloads and is used by more than 60% of the Fortune 500.

Agents will keep getting faster, and their actions will keep reaching deeper into the cloud. The companies that scale them with confidence will be the ones that put the controls in first: every agent known, owned, and tied to an identity; the risky actions stopped as they happen; and a record that holds up afterwards.

articles.title: Security briefing: October 2026
articles.context: The first public GitHub repository tracking the CVE appeared only hours after the fix, and exploitation attempts were confirmed within days
articles.full_text:
Attackers were definitely testing our cybersecurity best practices during Cybersecurity Awareness Month. A cloud region was knocked offline in Japan. Grocery stores across the US and Europe were either taken offline temporarily or lost produce. An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to breach an organization that was established to help others with vulnerability disclosure. And finally, there were well over one thousand vulnerability patches in a single day. No seriously. Vulnerability management was like walking into a burning building in October.

With that, let’s dive into this month’s security news.

Oct. 7: Ransomware takes down Japanese cloud infrastructure

A Japanese SoftBank subsidiary called IDC Frontier confirmed a ransomware attack began on October 7, impacting nearly 500 companies and local governments.

Allegedly, customers saw messages claiming 3.6PB of data was encrypted in seven minutes.

The ransomware group claims to have deleted snapshots.

This was in addition to other large-scale attacks across the country in October, including Burger King Japan, Nikkei, and Capcom.

Shared responsibility includes your own backups. Test restoring them somewhere that isn’t your provider.

Oct. 11: Hackers burn French fridges

Overnight, between October 11 and 12, hackers forced refrigerators in hundreds of grocery stores across France into continuous defrost mode.

For six hours, the refrigeration equipment was pushed to temperatures of 50°C (122°F).

The Danish manufacturer, Danfoss, said the stores were running outdated firmware or had reached end-of-life support, which left equipment exposed to the internet.

This caused fires and potentially tens of millions of dollars in spoiled food. Although the incident was due to operational equipment exposure, it’s a global wake-up call to the physical impact of supply chain attacks.

Oct. 20-21: Six Linux vulnerabilities dropped at once

Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent five Linux kernel reports to the Linux kernel security team and one report to the ConnMan mailing list, all of which went out to the broader public mailing lists.

ZDI-CAN-33367 is a local privilege escalation in skb_zerocopy() with a public proof of concept. It’s another gap in the Dirty Frag fix (CVE-2026-43284) from May.

Oct. 21: PHP2Shell

PHP shipped two emergency releases on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

An unauthenticated attacker can run code with HTTP requests alone, and researchers estimate 1.3 -1.9 million exposed hosts are potentially vulnerable.

Exploitation started before the patches existed. Amazon reported seeing an attempt on October 17. Organizations need to patch immediately, restart every PHP worker, and assume breach as they scan environments for signs of unauthorized access.

Oct. 21: Node2Shell

Node2Shell, also known as HTTP2Shell, landed on organizations’ radars after Node.js fixed an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder on October 21.

The first public GitHub repository tracking the CVE appeared only hours after the fix, and exploitation attempts were confirmed within days.

The decoder also ships in Bun, Python Brotli packages, and some Envoy configurations.

Additional Sysdig TRT findings

An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to exploit a vulnerability disclosure program

On October 2, Sysdig TRT published an initial blog on the breach of the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) on September 21.

The attacker exploited two vulnerabilities in the Zammad open source helpdesk tool. These were identified as CVE-2026-102489, a remote code execution flaw, and CVE-2026-102490, a local privilege escalation flaw.

Originally thought to be zero-days, Zammad said it received a report on CVE-2026-102489 in August, before the breach.

Pickle bypasses

On October 27, the Sysdig TRT published an analysis on using pickles to bypass model-loading defenses in machine learning.

Six documented CVE bypasses beat PyTorch weights_only, Keras safe_mode, and picklescan. The check and the loader disagreed about what the file was in each case.

Loading a pickle file executes the code inside it. That’s a design flaw, not a patchable bug, so the fix is in the formatting. Switch to safetensors where possible and use runtime to detect what happens after the pickle is loaded.

Also in the news

Microsoft patches a record 1,411 flaws: Vulnerability discovery is quickly outpacing security teams’ capability to remediate. KrebsOnSecurity said the prior month’s record of 972 patched flaws was 10 times a “normal” Microsoft patch load, and October dwarfed it. The increase is due to the internal use of AI platforms to find vulnerabilities within Microsoft products. Security teams need to prioritize reachability and exploitation. This month included one actively exploited zero-day (CVE-2026-96951), two publicly disclosed ones, and 70 critical flaws.

US and European grocery store operations disrupted: Ahold Delhaize confirmed a cybersecurity incident on October 12 after taking systems offline on October 11 to contain it. Albert Heijn, Etos, Gall & Gall, Delhaize, and Stop & Shop were some of the stores affected.

Nation-state threat actors using agentic AI: China-affiliated threat group Storm-0940 used agents to compromise ConnectWise customers, according to Microsoft on October 21. The group used the open source ARTEX framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants. In multiple cases, the actors moved from targeting to privileged cloud access in less than three hours.

Closing thoughts

Look at the clocks from this month. PHP2Shell was exploited four days before the patch. There was a PoC in a public repo for Node2Shell within hours. Storm-0940 went from targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. Patch what’s reasonable first, in a reasonable amount of time. But watch for what happens after an exploit is known. Attackers can’t hide behavior.

And we just wrapped Cybersecurity Awareness Month. If you want to take a breather and step away from vulnerabilities for just a moment, here’s a list of simple things you should be doing daily to avoid a breach.

To stay informed between our monthly wrap-ups, you can get the latest from the Sysdig TRT on our blog, or follow my bi-weekly security newsletter musings on LinkedIn.
